name: Xor-Grid Problem
description: Given a matrix $$$a$$$ of size $$$n \times m$$$, each cell of which contains a non-negative integer. The integer lying at the intersection of the $$$i$$$-th row and the $$$j$$$-th column of the matrix is called $$$a_{i,j}$$$. Let's define $$$f(i)$$$ and $$$g(j)$$$ as the XOR of all integers in the $$$i$$$-th row and the $$$j$$$-th column, respectively. In one operation, you can either: Select any row $$$i$$$, then assign $$$a_{i,j} := g(j)$$$ for each $$$1 \le j \le m$$$; or Select any column $$$j$$$, then assign $$$a_{i,j} := f(i)$$$ for each $$$1 \le i \le n$$$. An example of applying an operation on column $$$2$$$ of the matrix. In this example, as we apply an operation on column $$$2$$$, all elements in this column are changed: $$$a_{1,2} := f(1) = a_{1,1} \oplus a_{1,2} \oplus a_{1,3} \oplus a_{1,4} = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 0$$$ $$$a_{2,2} := f(2) = a_{2,1} \oplus a_{2,2} \oplus a_{2,3} \oplus a_{2,4} = 2 \oplus 3 \oplus 5 \oplus 7 = 3$$$ $$$a_{3,2} := f(3) = a_{3,1} \oplus a_{3,2} \oplus a_{3,3} \oplus a_{3,4} = 2 \oplus 0 \oplus 3 \oplus 0 = 1$$$ $$$a_{4,2} := f(4) = a_{4,1} \oplus a_{4,2} \oplus a_{4,3} \oplus a_{4,4} = 10 \oplus 11 \oplus 12 \oplus 16 = 29$$$ You can apply the operations any number of times. Then, we calculate the $$$\textit{beauty}$$$ of the final matrix by summing the absolute differences between all pairs of its adjacent cells. More formally, $$$\textit{beauty}(a) = \sum|a_{x,y} - a_{r,c}|$$$ for all cells $$$(x, y)$$$ and $$$(r, c)$$$ if they are adjacent. Two cells are considered adjacent if they share a side. Find the minimum $$$\textit{beauty}$$$ among all obtainable matrices.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 250$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le n, m \le 15$$$) — the number of rows and columns of $$$a$$$, respectively. The next $$$n$$$ lines, each containing $$$m$$$ integers $$$a_{i,1}, a_{i,2}, \ldots, a_{i,m}$$$ ($$$0 \le a_{i,j} \lt 2^{20}$$$) — description of the matrix $$$a$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$(n^2 + m^2)$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$500$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer $$$b$$$ — the smallest possible $$$\textit{beauty}$$$ of the matrix.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1993E — Xor-Grid Problem [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
